name: Western Panjabi
confidence_why: No first-hand source states where single-word stress falls in this language: Varma 1936 says only that it 'agrees with Panjabi' and describes compound stress, Wilson 1899 notes accent in one verb paradigm, Grierson 1919 presupposes an accented syllable without locating it, and the weight-sensitive rule of Hussain, Proctor, Harvey and Demuth 2020 describes urban Lyallpuri Punjabi, a Majhi-type variety, not the Shahpuri, Dhanni or Jatki dialects of this record.

Calcutta: Superintendent of Government Printing. xii+579 pp. ('Lahnda or Western Panjabi': introduction and 'Sketch of Lahnda Grammar', Pronunciation pp. 246-251).
tone_statements.quote: In other positions, i.e. when it is not at the beginning of a word or preceding the accented syllable, it is hardly audible or may be altogether inaudible, but it strongly raises the pitch of the preceding vowel, often altering the whole tone of the word. Thus, Idh, bring down, is very different in sound from Id, attach, although the h in the former is often quite inaudible. Similarly, the first a in Id kid, speedy, is pronounced in a high tone, while in Mid, black, it has the ordinary tone, although the h in the former word is not itself sounded.
tone_statements.locator: LSI vol. VIII pt. 1, 'Sketch of Lahnda Grammar', Pronunciation (letter h), p. 251
tone_statements.summary: Standard Lahnda (Shahpuri): Punjabi-type word tone — postvocalic/medial h and voiced-aspirate h are lost or weakened and leave a high (raised) pitch on the preceding vowel, giving tonal minimal pairs (lāh vs lā, kāhlā vs kālā); word accent also present; no toneme inventory stated.

audit.recode_to: no reclassification. Keep not determinable for the Glottolog-tree object (Shahpuri/Dhanni/Jatki Lahnda). Annotate: (i) identity/crosswalk note that ISO 639-3 pnb as used by Ethnologue and by Hussain et al. 2020 JIPA ('Punjabi (Western, ISO-639-3 pnb)') covers Majhi-type Pakistani Punjabi (Lahore, Faisalabad/Lyallpur, Gujranwala, Sahiwal), which Glottolog files under panj1256 (majh1252), not under west2386; (ii) cite Hussain et al. 2020 pp. 293-294 alongside Bashir & Conners 2019 pp. 50-52 in the secondary-stress rule as out-of-tree (in-ISO) evidence of the Panjabi quantity-sensitive rule that Varma 1936 p. 64 says Lahnda single-word stress 'agrees with'; (iii) roster note for the compilers: panj1256 (Eastern Panjabi incl. Majhi/Lahore) has no row, so the Punjabi quantity-sensitive system is coded nowhere; the fix is a new panj1256 record (B&C 2019, Hussain et al. 2020, Bhatia 1993, Dhillon 2010), not a reclassify of west2386.

For the narrow Glottolog-tree languoid nothing better was found (Glottolog lists only Wilson 1899, Bailey 1904, Mullick 2003; CrossRef/archive. Smirnov 1975 unseen;org, Open Library and Cambridge Core directly). (3) The risk is identity, not misquotation: west238

sources.citation: Hussain, Qandeel, Michael Proctor, Mark Harvey & Katherine Demuth. 2020 (online 2019). Punjabi (Lyallpuri variety). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 50(2): 282-297. doi:10.1017/S0025100319000021 (open access).
sources.quote: 'Stress is not contrastive in Lyallpuri Punjabi. All words have at least one stressed syllable. Stress assignment is sensitive to syllable weight ... Three categories of syllable weight ... light (monomoraic: (C)V ...), heavy (bimoraic ...), and superheavy (trimoraic: (C)VC ... or (C)VCC ...). In disyllabic words, the leftmost superheavy syllable is stressed ... If there is no superheavy syllable, then the penultimate syllable is stressed. In trisyllabic words ... stress is always placed on the penultimate or antepenultimate syllable, but not on the final syllable.' Also: 'Tones always align w
sources.locator: pp. 293-294, section 'Stress and tone', example table (7), fn. 5-6

sources.citation: Bailey, T. Grahame. 1914. A Panjabi Phonetic Reader (London Phonetic Readers). London: University of London Press. archive.org cu31924023155298 (scanned).
sources.quote: Tones 'occur in stressed syllables only'; 'When several syllables normally having the same kind of tone come together, it is customary in rapid conversation to pronounce the tone only in the most strongly stressed syllables'; 'The mark ' means that the following syllable is stressed. It has been very sparingly used.' No placement rule. (Glottolog files Bailey's 1904 Wazirabad grammar under west2386, but Wazirabad/Gujranwala speech is Majhi-side; carried only as context.)
